opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think metric choice should shape those claims a lot more than it often does, and that was really the heart of the work we did on whether emergent abilities are a mirage.

What we found is that many of the dramatic, sharp jumps people pointed to as "emergence" lined up with the researcher's choice of metric. If you use something nonlinear or discontinuous, like exact-match accuracy or multiple-choice grade, you're scoring all-or-nothing. A model can be getting steadily better at the underlying task, with per-token error going down smoothly as you scale, and an exact-match metric will show essentially zero until suddenly it doesn't. Get one token wrong in a five-digit addition problem and you get no credit. So the curve looks like a cliff even when the capability underneath is changing gradually.

When we took the same model outputs and scored them with continuous or linear metrics, like token edit distance or Brier score, a lot of those sharp transitions turned into smooth, predictable curves. We could also go the other way and induce what looked like emergence in vision models, where nobody had claimed it, just by picking the right harsh metric.

So my practical advice is a few things. First, if you're going to claim an ability emerges, check whether it survives a change of metric. If it vanishes when you switch to a continuous measure, you're probably seeing a property of your measurement, not of the model. Second, think about resolution. Small evaluation sets and few model sizes can make things look abrupt simply because you can't measure small improvements. Third, be explicit about what question you're asking. Sometimes the all-or-nothing metric really is what matters for deployment. If you need the full answer right, exact match is the honest metric. But then the claim should be "the usefulness for this task crosses a threshold," not "the model acquired a new capability out of nowhere."

I want to be careful here, though. We weren't saying nothing interesting ever happens with scale, or that every instance of emergence is an artifact. The point is that the burden of proof should be on showing the discontinuity is in the model and not in the ruler. That matters for science, but also for safety and policy. If we think capabilities appear unpredictably, that leads to one set of conclusions. If many of them are actually predictable with the right measurement, that's good news, because it means we can forecast and prepare better.

r001.rationale: The response says harsh metrics can make gradual improvement look like a sharp cliff, but it does not clearly claim that this can make progress seem unpredictable to a lay observer.

r002.rationale: It connects metric-dependent emergence claims to safety and policy conclusions, explaining that perceiving capabilities as unpredictable can lead to different conclusions than recognizing predictable progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So this is something I've thought about a lot, and the short version is that I think metric choice should be front and center in any claim about emergence, because in many of the cases we looked at, the metric is doing most of the work.

Let me back up. The standard emergence story goes something like: you scale a model up, performance is flat, flat, flat, and then suddenly it jumps. And people interpret that jump as the model having acquired some qualitatively new capability. That's a strong claim, and it has real consequences for how we think about safety, about predictability, about what we can anticipate as we keep scaling.

What we found when we dug into it is that a huge fraction of those reported emergent abilities show up under metrics that are discontinuous or nonlinear in the thing the model is actually doing. Exact match is the classic example. If you ask a model to do five-digit arithmetic and you score it as right or wrong on the whole answer, then a model that gets four of five digits right scores exactly the same as one that gets zero right. So as the model improves smoothly on a per-token basis, your metric sits at zero until the model crosses a threshold where it gets everything right, and then it shoots up. That looks like emergence, but it's an artifact of the scoring. If you switch to something like token edit distance, or you look at the per-token probability, the curve is smooth and predictable. Same model, same outputs, completely different story.

So my position is that if you want to claim emergence, you have a burden of proof that includes showing the behavior is robust to metric choice. If a sharp transition appears under accuracy but disappears under a continuous metric, then I don't think you've found something about the model. You've found something about your measurement.

Now, I want to be careful here, because people sometimes take this as "emergence is fake," and that's not what I'm saying. There may well be genuine phase transitions in what models can do. Things like in-context learning or certain reasoning behaviors might really involve the model learning a different kind of computation. What I'm saying is that the evidence bar should be higher, and that a lot of what's been reported doesn't clear it once you control for the metric.

There's also a sample size issue tied up in this. Many of these benchmarks have small test sets, and when you're measuring something at the far tail, like a model that's barely above zero accuracy, you can't resolve small improvements. You get zero, zero, zero, and then a nonzero number, and that reads as a jump even if the underlying ability was growing all along. More data points, or a more resolution-friendly metric, would let you see the gradual trend.

Why does this matter beyond the academic question? Because the policy and safety conversation has leaned heavily on emergence as a reason to expect surprises. If capabilities really do appear unpredictably, that's a different risk landscape than if they come online smoothly and you could have forecast them from smaller models. I think the honest answer is that for most of what we've measured, the latter is closer to true, and that's actually good news for the field. It means we can build evaluation suites that give us early warning rather than being blindsided.

So, practically, what I'd like to see is that whenever someone reports emergent behavior, they report it under multiple metrics, including at least one continuous one, they show the per-example distribution rather than just the aggregate, and they're explicit about whether the claim survives those changes. If it does, great, that's interesting and worth studying. If it doesn't, then we should describe it as what it is, which is a thresholding effect of our scoring rule, not a new capability springing into existence.

r001.rationale: The response explains that discontinuous metrics can make smooth improvement look like a sudden jump, but does not clearly claim this makes progress unpredictable to a lay observer.

r002.rationale: It links emergence claims to the policy and safety discussion, explains that metric choice can change whether capabilities appear sudden, and calls for reporting multiple metrics to support those claims.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to be careful to distinguish emergence in a capability from emergence in the way we measure that capability. Suppose you evaluate a task using exact match: the model gets a one only if the entire answer is correct, and a zero otherwise. The model might be improving steadily, but that metric can make its performance look like it suddenly jumps once it crosses a particular threshold.

If you use a more graded measure—how much of the answer is correct, for example—you might see a much smoother curve. That doesn’t mean the exact-match metric is wrong. For some applications, getting the whole answer right really is what matters. But it changes the claim you can make. A sudden improvement in task success isn’t necessarily evidence of a sudden change in the underlying capability.

So I’d want to see whether the result holds across reasonable metrics, how sensitive it is to the evaluation setup, and what uncertainty there is around those measurements. Emergence should be something we investigate and explain, rather than something we infer from a single plot.

r001.rationale: The response says exact match can make steady improvement look like a sudden jump, but it does not communicate that this can appear unpredictable to a lay observer.

r002.rationale: The response discusses risks of inferring emergence from one plot but does not connect metric choice to risks for policymaking.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the metric has to be part of the claim. When we say a capability is emergent, we usually mean that it seems to appear suddenly as we increase model scale. But what appears suddenly may be the score, depending on how we measure success.

For example, if you score an answer as correct only when every part is right, you can see a sharp jump even when the underlying model is improving gradually. A metric that gives partial credit might show a much smoother curve for the same models.

That doesn’t mean the improvement isn’t real or useful. If your application requires an entirely correct answer, that threshold matters. But it’s a different claim to say, “The model crossed a useful threshold,” versus, “The model acquired a fundamentally new capability.”

So I’d want to see how robust the result is across reasonable metrics, along with uncertainty and enough measurements around the apparent transition. If the emergence disappears when you change the scoring rule, that should narrow the claim we make about what’s happening inside the model.

r001.rationale: The response explains that strict all-or-nothing scoring can make gradual improvement look like a sharp jump, but it does not say the change appears unpredictable to a lay observer.

r002.rationale: The response discusses how metric choice affects emergence claims but does not mention risks for policymaking.
